Machine-learning models can encode biophysical principles and guide the generation of protein-based materials. When combined with high-throughput experimentation, generative AI can integrate sequence design, structure prediction, and functional validation into closed-loop workflows. These workflows can accelerate the development of programmable biomaterials. This review summarizes AI-driven advances in protein-based materials and emerging links with autonomous robotics.

title: Dark energy: the cost of function in protein evolution.
authors: Galpern, Ezequiel A; Caamano, Federico; Sanchez, Ignacio E; Ferreiro, Diego U
abstract: The evolutionary fate of proteins is driven by both folding stability and biological function, dual constraints that often conflict, creating frustration and imposing functional costs beyond stability. These costs can be captured by a 'dark energy': the difference between the evolutionary energy of protein sequences and their physical folding energy. Recent advances in deep mutational scanning, protein language models, and inverse-folding models have enabled the quantification of dark energy across the protein universe. We review the computational and experimental approaches that disentangle folding and function at scale, revealing a dark energy component and providing new insights into how biological information flows from sequence to structure to function and back to sequence.

title: Modeling Phase Separation in Polymer-Derived Silicon Carbonitride Ceramics through Extended Machine Learning Molecular Dynamics.
authors: Mortier, Fabien; Cadars, Sylvian; Masson, Olivier; Boero, Mauro; Ori, Guido; Wang, Yun; Bernard, Samuel; Bouzid, Assil
abstract: Polymer-derived ceramics combine the thermal stability of ceramics with the versatile properties of carbon domains, but modeling their atomic-scale evolution during processing remains elusive because of the limitations of traditional computational methods. To address this issue, here, we develop and apply a machine learning interatomic potential for hydrogen-containing silicon carbonitride-based (SiCNH) ceramics, trained on a diversified database of over 9000 configurations horizontal line including amorphous models, high-temperature states, surfaces, and crystal structure predictions horizontal line to capture the full complexity of these materials. This potential enables large-scale molecular dynamics simulations of 8000-atom systems, revealing the atomic-scale evolution of the polymer-derived ceramic during thermal treatment. A key result of this work is the occurrence of a phase separation, where carbon domains progressively nucleate from the amorphous SiCN matrix during thermal processing, forming distinct graphene-like sheets while preserving the integrity of the ceramic network. The resulting models reproduce the experimental atomic pair distribution functions, supporting our approach and providing microscopic explanations for the material combination of the ceramic and graphitic properties. In this process, defective 5- and/or 7-member carbon rings mediate the transformation to stable 6-member aromatic structures. These findings provide atomic-scale information about the thermal stability and structural transformation pathways of polymer-derived ceramics and demonstrate the applicability of the methodology to complex amorphous systems at experimentally relevant scales.

title: Cross-linking mass spectrometry guided structure prediction of disordered Encephalitozoon hellem proteins.
authors: Weyer, Elizabeth; Wang, Yongliang; Tomita, Tadakimi; Madrid-Aliste, Carlos; Nandigrami, Prithviraj; Fiser, Andras; Sidoli, Simone; Aguilan, Jennifer T; Han, Bing; Weiss, Louis M
abstract: Microsporidia such as Encephalitozoon hellem are obligate intracellular human parasites that remain genetically intractable, limiting the functional characterization of their proteomes. Experimental structural studies are challenging, as many proteins in microsporidia comprise a large percentage of disordered regions. Computational structural studies based on homology-based modeling and the use of deep-learning algorithms for microsporidian proteins also remain limited because most have little to no sequence similarity to proteins with solved structures. To address these limitations, we developed an approach that incorporates cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) data into structure prediction. XL-MS data provide upper-bound distance constraints that can be incorporated into protein deep-learning-based modeling and subsequent docking. Using this approach, we generated a model of two interacting E. hellem spore wall proteins, spore wall protein 1B (Swp1b) and endospore protein 1 (EnP1), which have no clear homologs outside of microsporidia and contain several disordered regions. These proteins are abundant spore wall proteins of microsporidia and previously were not known to interact with one another. The resulting model not only is consistent with the experimental cross-links used to generate the model but was also subsequently confirmed by independently generated XL-MS data. The described AlphaLink-Modeller framework for structure prediction is particularly well suited to proteins with limited homology and/or substantial flexible regions, given that they adopt a defined structural state within a biological context, thereby extending integrative modeling approaches to previously inaccessible targets. IMPORTANCE: In this article, we demonstrate an improved method for the prediction of the structure of protein complexes with no clear homologs and a considerable number of disordered regions. This is significant because these types of proteins are critical to understanding the biology of organisms, yet model generation of these classes has been inaccessible. The method incorporates experimental data obtained from cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) into the modeling process, providing a method to integrate such experimental data into computational modeling of the structure of proteins and protein interactions. For this paper, we have used this method for predicting the structure of two highly abundant Encephalitozoon hellem proteins in the spore wall that are important for host cell infection due to this pathogen of humans and other vertebrates.

title: Unlocking the molecular mechanisms of bamboo-based remediation of hazardous contaminants: macromolecular interactions, transport pathways, and predictive approaches.
authors: Ali, Muhammad Hayder; Hameed, Muhammad Ashir; Cong, Ma; Malik, Aqsa; Chen, Qibin; Liu, Shiliang
abstract: Bamboo presents an unusual combination of rapid biomass production and diverse molecular mechanisms for capturing, transforming, and sequestering hazardous contaminants. However, the existing investigations have predominantly focused on bulk removal efficiencies and tissue-level accumulation profiles, whereas the molecular determinants governing these processes remain critically underexplored. This review systematically synthesizes the structure-function relationships of key bamboo-derived macromolecules including cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, membrane transport proteins such as heavy metal ATPases (HMAs), ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters, natural resistance-associated macrophage proteins (NRAMPs), and zinc-regulated/iron-regulated transporter-like proteins (ZIPs), as well as oxidative enzymes such as laccases and peroxidases. Specific emphasis is placed on the molecular features that drive contaminant adsorption, transport, sequestration, and degradation. Particular attention is given to surface functional groups, aromatic domains, conserved transporter motifs, and catalytic metal centers. A critical appraisal of the current literature reveals substantial knowledge gaps, particularly in molecular-weight distributions, three-dimensional conformational states, binding affinities, and direct physicochemical interactions between bamboo-derived macromolecules and hazardous pollutants. To address these limitations, we propose an integrative framework combining proteomics, AI-assisted structure prediction, molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and quantitative binding assays to uncover the molecular basis of bamboo-pollutant interactions. Future breakthroughs will require the synergistic integration of rigorous structural characterization and direct interaction studies to move from descriptive associations toward predictive structure-function relationships. By consolidating dispersed knowledge and outlining prioritized research agendas, this review furnishes a conceptual framework to advance bamboo-based remediation from descriptive observational studies toward predictive, mechanism-driven strategies for hazardous contaminant management and environmental risk reduction.

title: Engineering a hemoglobin variant with enhanced stability and oxygen affinity using a protein language model.
authors: Shityakov, Sergey; Novikov, Alexander S; Skorb, Ekaterina V; Dandekar, Thomas
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Engineered hemoglobin variants offer therapeutic promise for artificial blood substitutes and oxygen therapeutics, but rational design is constrained by protein stability and heme-binding. Protein language models (pLMs) predict mutation fitness, yet their integration with biophysical validation remains limited. METHODS: We developed a hybrid pipeline combining pLM (ESM3) with molecular docking, Monte Carlo simulation, molecular dynamics, MM-GBSA/PBSA binding free energy calculations, and density functional theory (DFT) to engineer a stabilized hemoglobin variant (esmHb) with enhanced oxygen affinity, benchmarking against the clinically characterized Hb Fort de France mutation (alpha45 His-->Arg). RESULTS: ESM3 accurately assessed the fitness effect of the Hb Fort de France mutation and generated structurally stable esmHb models. Compared with the wild-type variant (wtHb), esmHb exhibited improved thermodynamic stability (DeltaG: -18.48 vs. -12.22 kcal/mol), increased heme-binding affinity (DeltaGbind: -11.79 vs. -8.42 kcal/mol), and greater thermodynamic favorability of oxidation according to DFT calculations (DeltaE: -173.1 vs. -149.9 kcal/mol). MM-GBSA and MM-PBSA binding free energy calculations further supported improved protein-heme and protein-protein interactions, with esmHb showing more favorable values in both implicit solvation models. Statistical significance (p < 0.05) was reached for protein-protein interactions via both methods and for protein-heme interactions via MM-PBSA. We interpret the MM-GBSA results as a suggestive trend rather than definitive evidence. DISCUSSION: This work establishes a generalizable framework for pLM-driven protein engineering applicable to therapeutic Hb variants and beyond.

title: Advances and applications of engineered protein therapeutics and their role in precision medicine.
authors: Aldossary, Wadha; Alqahtani, Nada; Asiri, Layla; Alkhurayef, Noora; Alagl, Samar; Alturki, Sana; Saad, Duha; Al Yahya, Mashael; Al-Harthi, Samah
abstract: Proteins are a vital class of biomolecules. They play essential roles in biological processes, including building cellular structures, forming cellular channels and receptors, catalyzing biological reactions, transporting molecules, and contributing to immune defense mechanisms. Advances in protein engineering have enabled the genetic modification of naturally occurring proteins, using recombinant deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) technology, leading to the development of therapeutic proteins with enhanced specificity, stability, and clinical performance. Despite the rapid growth of engineered biologics, a comprehensive understanding of how these innovations intersect with precision medicine remains limited. This review addresses this gap by summarizing the major contemporary approaches used in therapeutic protein engineering, including directed evolution, rational design, and de novo protein design, and by analyzing their roles in enabling patient-tailored interventions. It provides an integrated overview of the clinical applications of engineered therapeutic proteins across key medical fields, supported by a list of U.S. Food and Drug Administration- and European Medicines Agency-approved protein therapeutics from 2020 to 2025. The review further provides a comparative perspective on major protein engineering strategies, highlighting their relative advantages and limitations, while examining differences in clinical translation across major disease areas. By combining technological advances with disease-specific applications, this review offers a perspective that has not been fully developed in the literature. Finally, the review discusses the current challenges affecting the implementation of precision medicine, including immunogenicity, regulatory constraints, and ethical considerations, and outlines future directions, such as artificial intelligence-guided protein design, targeted protein degradation, and personalized vaccine development. Collectively, these insights highlight the expanding role of engineered proteins in shaping the next-generation of precision therapeutics and emphasize the growing importance of integrating multidisciplinary approaches to advance therapeutic innovation in modern clinical practice.

title: Molecular characterization and pathogenicity stratification of YWHAG missense variants in developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.
authors: Liu, Wen-Hui; Zhou, Juan; Zhu, Zhong-Yan; Wen, Qian-Ru; Zhang, Si-Qi; Ding, Yan; Meng, Heng
abstract: BACKGROUND: Variants in YWHAG cause severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) with early-onset seizures. Rapid and precise clinical classification of its missense variants presents a substantial challenge. This study sought to explore YWHAG spatiotemporal expression-pathogenicity correlation and reliable pathogenicity indicators for its variants to promote clinical genetic diagnosis. METHODS: In this study, 55 YWHAG missense variants were curated, including 17 pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants that met ACMG guideline criteria and 38 benign variants from gnomAD. We performed protein structure modeling, spatiotemporal expression profiling, single-cell transcriptome analysis, PPI network construction, and functional enrichment analysis. We also evaluated 34 pathogenicity prediction tools using accuracy, balanced accuracy, AUC, and MCC. RESULTS: Protein structure modeling revealed that hydrogen bond alterations occurred in both pathogenic and benign YWHAG variants, which could not reliably distinguish the two groups. YWHAG was highly expressed in the central nervous system with three distinct developmental peaks, shifting from both excitatory and inhibitory neurons to predominantly excitatory neurons during cerebral organoid maturation. The YWHAG protein regulated the MAPK, PI3K-Akt, Hippo pathways and cell cycle progression. Among the 34 evaluated tools, deep learning and ensemble algorithms outperformed traditional conservation-based predictors, with MetaSVM showing the best overall performance, MetaLR achieving excellent specificity and ESM1b attaining the highest AUC value. CONCLUSION: Meta-predictors may effectively predict YWHAG missense variant pathogenicity, and YWHAG spatiotemporal expression aligns with its DEE pathogenic role. These computational tools may provide reliable support for the pathogenicity assessment of YWHAG variants in clinical genetic diagnosis.

title: Uncoupling of the allosteric signalling network in the beta(1)-adrenergic receptor by a negative allosteric modulator.
authors: Harman, Thomas H; Noel, Timothy; Nokhbehzaim, Ali; Pearce, Abigail; Jones, Andrew J Y; Saji, Anjana; Harris, Matthew; Vege, Venkat S; Chandran, Aneesh; Leroy, Pierre; Al-Sabah, Suleiman; Ladds, Graham; Nietlispach, Daniel
abstract: Allosteric modulation is a fundamental aspect of G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) regulation where molecules that bind to alternative sites outside the orthosteric pocket alter agonist-induced signalling responses. The advantages of allosteric modulators over traditional orthosteric agonists have positioned them as highly promising therapeutic agents. GPCRs exist in tuneable equilibria between multiple functional states, yet the ways in which allosteric modulators reshape these equilibria remain incompletely understood. Here we characterise how changes to the allosteric signalling network influence the conformational dynamics of the beta(1)-adrenergic receptor (beta(1)AR) through mutations at the E130(3.41) position or using the negative allosteric modulator, AS408. Both act through a known transmembrane (TM)3-TM4-TM5 site, reducing signalling to similar extents, but through distinct molecular mechanisms as revealed by pharmacological assays, MD simulations, and solution nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. E130(3.41) mutations reduce agonist-stimulated signalling as a side chain-dependent rheostat, shifting receptor equilibria to populate states with weaker G protein affinities. In contrast, AS408 uncouples the intracellular region of beta(1)AR from the influence of the orthosteric pocket and reduces G protein coupling by adoption of an alternative signalling-incompetent intracellular surface arrangement. Our investigations emphasise the relevance of mechanistic understanding in drug development and the importance of dynamics in GPCR allostery.

title: DNA-BFN: Bayesian Flow Networks for Generative Modeling of Regulatory DNA Sequences.
authors: Yu, Han; Du, Qixiu; Wei, Lei; Wang, Xiaowo
abstract: MOTIVATION: Designing regulatory DNA sequences is challenging due to their discrete nucleotide alphabet and complex higher-order dependencies underlying regulatory function. Many existing generative models, particularly diffusion-based approaches, learn by injecting stochastic noise into sequences and training denoising processes, which can distort discrete sequence structure and weaken biological constraints. RESULTS: Here, we introduce DNA Bayesian Flow Networks (DNA-BFN), a generative framework that models regulatory DNA sequences through iterative Bayesian updates of per-position nucleotide distributions. By directly modeling per-position categorical beliefs, DNA-BFN realizes a diffusion-like generative process without explicitly perturbing discrete nucleotide sequences, enabling fully differentiable training while preserving discrete sequence structure. Across eight regulatory sequence datasets spanning diverse species, scales, and sequence lengths, DNA-BFN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, faithfully preserves sequence feature statistics and regulatory patterns, enables few-shot sequence design, and achieves faster sampling efficiency. These results show that framing sequence generation as progressive uncertainty reduction in probability space provides an effective and generalizable approach for nucleotide sequence design. AVAILABILITY: The software and its source code are publicly available at https://github.com/WangLabTHU/DNA-BFN. The dataset, source code and model weights are available in the Zenodo repository: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20177972. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: MARDy 2.0: a platform for exploring and analysing antifungal resistance mutations.
authors: Webber, Joe; Gifford, Hugh; Rhodes, Johanna; Farrer, Rhys A
abstract: MOTIVATION: The rising incidence of antifungal drug resistance represents a major and growing threat to global public health and food security. Therefore, understanding the genetic and molecular mechanisms that underpin antifungal resistance is essential for both clinical management and agricultural disease control. RESULTS: We present MARDy 2.0, an updated platform replacing the original Mycology Antifungal Resistance Database. MARDy 2.0 provides an interactive platform for exploring antifungal resistance data from the community resource FungAMR, and protein structures from UniProtKB or predicted structures using AlphaFold. The platform provides enhanced tools for data exploration and analysis and is freely accessible via an interactive web interface that supports search filtering and downloads, BLAST-based sequence similarity searches, an experimental natural-language query interface for exploratory analysis, a mutation plot for visualising mutations in a protein context, and structural predictions showing mutation locations. MARDy 2.0 provides a platform to facilitate research into antifungal resistance evolution, surveillance, and mitigation strategies. MARDy should be used and cited alongside the underlying resources it integrates, FungAMR. AVAILABILITY: Accessible at https://mardy.net.

title: X-linked novel hemizygous ADGRG2 variants associated with male factor infertility.
authors: Yuan, Yuwei; Li, Yong; Lu, Wenqing; Peng, Zhendong; Deng, Lei; Lin, Xinle; Liu, Lin; Meng, Lanlan; Tan, Chen; Lin, Ge; Zhang, Qianjun; Tan, Yue-Qiu; Zhang, Huan; He, Wenbin; Li, Huanzhu; Hu, Liang; Tu, Chaofeng
journal: Journal of assisted reproduction and genetics
abstract: PURPOSE: To screen for ADGRG2 gene mutations in CFTR-negative patients with male infertility or congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBAVD), and to assess the feasibility and outcomes of intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) for achieving successful pregnancies in this population. METHODS: Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed in 133 infertile men with obstructive azoospermia (OA). Sanger sequencing were conducted on peripheral blood samples collected from nine patients with ADGRG2 variants. The AlphaFold database and PyMOL software were used to predict the 3D structure of the mutant ADGRG2 protein. In vitro assays were conducted to assess the functional impact of the identified ADGRG2 variants. In addition, we also conducted a retrospective analysis of the clinical assisted reproductive information of these patients. RESULTS: We identified eight ADGRG2 hemizygous pathogenic variants in nine unrelated patients with CBAVD from 133 OA men: one splicing variant (c.1839 + 1G > A), three frameshift variants (c.2956_2957del: p.M986Vfs*2; c.2396dupT: p.L799Ffs*18 and c.895delA: p.I299Ffs*12), two nonsense variants (c.2473C > T: p.R825* and c.2971G > T: p.E991*), and two missense variants (c.510G > C: p.E170D and c.549C > G: p.S183R). All ADGRG2 variants-affected individuals presented with azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia. All of these variants were absent or rare in public databases. 3D protein structure modeling predicted that ADGRG2 variants lead to alterations in the spatial conformation of the protein. In vitro experiments further confirmed that these variants result in the production of truncated proteins or reduced protein levels. Notably, four patients undergoing ICSI treatment achieved successful fertilization and pregnancy. CONCLUSION: Our findings established ADGRG2 variants cause male infertility and may be the etiology of CBAVD, expanding the associated mutational spectrum and reinforcing the gene's critical role in male fertility, thereby supporting the integration of comprehensive ADGRG2 screening into clinical practice to enhance genetic and reproductive counseling for affected patients.

title: APR-Score: Identification and Scoring of Aggregation-prone Regions in Protein Sequences.
authors: Kaushik, Rahul; Launey, Thomas
abstract: Protein aggregation is a critical phenomenon associated with numerous neurodegenerative and systemic diseases. Understanding the propensity of proteins to aggregate is essential for unraveling the molecular basis of these disorders and for the design and engineering of novel proteins, as well as for modulating the activity/stability of enzymatic proteins. Here, we present APR-Score, a novel machine learning-based computational method designed to identify aggregation-prone regions within protein sequences. APR-Score leverages a combination of sequence-based features to predict regions of proteins that are prone to aggregation. It harnessed the information embedded in compiled sequence and structural features to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy. The method was evaluated through rigorous cross-validation on the training dataset and further validated on an independent test dataset. APR-Score demonstrated robustness and reliability in distinguishing aggregation-prone regions from non-aggregating ones, achieving a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.77, precision of 0.89, and F1-Score of 0.87. This tool offers significant value for researchers investigating protein aggregation-related diseases, as it can expedite the identification of aggregation-prone regions, thereby aiding the development of targeted therapies and diagnostic tools. Moreover, computational protein design and engineering efforts can be facilitated by APR-Score-based identification and screening of aggregation-prone protein sequences. APR-Score is available at https://github.com/TII-BRC/APR-Score.

title: Elucidating the relationship between protein amide I, II, and III bands and secondary structures by localized anharmonic vibrational calculations.
authors: Matsuyama, Nao; Yagi, Kiyoshi
abstract: The amide I, II, and III spectra of the insulin dimer and ubiquitin were investigated using our recently developed localized, second-order vibrational quasi-degenerate perturbation theory (VQDPT2) combined with quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics calculations. By averaging over ten snapshots from molecular dynamics trajectories, we confirmed that the computed spectra converged to a sufficient degree. Although the method has intrinsic limitations due to the neglect of vibrational coupling between neighboring amide groups, we found that the method provides a useful basis for spectral analysis of these proteins. The analysis of the averaged amide I, II, and III bands revealed that, for both proteins, the amide II and III peak positions tend to be closely associated with the coil contribution, whereas the origin of the amide I maximum is more protein dependent. The calculated amide I and III frequencies of the coil structures showed good agreement with experimental values. The spectra of each secondary structure were further subdivided according to the type of hydrogen bonding within the secondary structure. For structurally constrained alpha-helix and beta-sheet structures, hydrogen-bond-dependent amide I frequency shifts were found to correlate with changes in the amide dihedral angles (O=C-N-H). Localized VQDPT2 enables direct interpretation of amide band shifts associated with conformational changes and provides a deeper understanding of the structural origin responsible for these band shifts.

title: Loss of the Asn333 high-mannose N-glycan impairs ACP3 folding and drives disease-associated dysfunction.
authors: Manabe, Noriyoshi; Itoh, Kazuyoshi; Ohno, Shiho; Miura, Ayumi; Miyata, Aika; Yashima, Sora; Komatsu, Sachiko; Fujimura, Tsutomu; Hanamatsu, Hisatoshi; Furukawa, Jun-Ichi; Angata, Kiyohiko; Togayachi, Akira; Aoki-Kinoshita, Kiyoko F; Akimoto, Yoshihiro; Kaname, Tadashi; Nishihara, Shoko; Yamaguchi, Yoshiki
abstract: Missense mutations disrupting N-glycosylation motifs can perturb protein folding and trafficking, yet the site-specific contributions of individual N-glycans to proteostasis remain poorly defined. Here, we delineated the functional hierarchy of three N-glycosylation sites in human prostatic acid phosphatase (ACP3). Glycoproteomic analysis showed that Asn94 and Asn220 carry predominantly complex-type N-glycans, whereas Asn333 is enriched in high-mannose structures. Glycan-deficient N94Q and N220Q variants were efficiently secreted and retained phosphatase activity, whereas N333Q and T335M accumulated intracellularly, formed endoplasmic reticulum aggregates, and lacked enzymatic activity. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the Asn333 high-mannose glycan forms persistent hydrogen-bond networks with surrounding residues and exhibits markedly reduced conformational flexibility, supporting a non-redundant structural role. Individuals harboring a heterozygous p.T335M variant presented severe neurodevelopmental abnormalities, linking Asn333 glycan loss to proteostasis failure in vivo. These findings establish a site-specific glycan-protein stabilizing mechanism with broad implications in glycoprotein folding and human disease.

title: Deep learning coupled with scalable domain-specific structural validation expands RNA virus discovery from metatranscriptomes.
authors: Luo, Gaoyang; Zang, Zelin; Yuan, Ling; Zhou, Jingbo; Dong, Ao; Huang, Yufei; Li, Stan Z; Ju, Feng
abstract: The discovery of RNA viruses from metatranscriptomic data remains challenging due to extreme sequence divergence and length heterogeneity, ranging from massive polyproteins to short assembly artifacts. We present Rider, a two-stage framework that synergizes deep representation learning with scalable domain-specific structural validation. In the first stage, Rider leverages a compact pretrained protein language model to broadly detect highly divergent viral signals. To overcome the inherent input length limitations of language models and accurately capture catalytic core domains, the second stage employs an overlapping sliding-window structure prediction strategy. These structures are then aligned against our curated database of non-redundant RdRp (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) domains. This domain-centric design detects RdRp domains embedded within long polyproteins and truncated fragments. Across >10,000 metatranscriptomes spanning diverse ecosystems, Rider achieves sensitivity comparable to LucaProt, recalling >99% of previously cataloged RNA viruses. Rider identifies thousands of deeply divergent sequences and clades that elude existing methods. In a human inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) cohort, Rider agrees with other methods in detecting RNA viruses while extending detection to divergent lineages, providing a scalable pipeline for global RNA virome exploration.

title: Structural and functional insights into a Zn(2+)-transporting P-type ATPase.
authors: Lyu, Pin; Longhin, Elena; Sabzian-Molaei, Fatemeh; Montalvillo Ortega, Fernando; Li, Ping; Wang, Kaituo; Duelli, Annette; Al-Jubair, Tamim; Ahmed Hotiana, Hajira; Ramos Becares, Eva; Croll, Tristan; Meloni, Gabriele; Andersson, Magnus; Bagenholm, Viktoria; Gourdon, Pontus
abstract: Zinc is essential for life yet toxic in excess, rendering homeostatic control vital for all organisms. Transition metal transporting P-type (P(IB)-) ATPase proteins are critical for this balance but remain poorly understood at the molecular level. Here, we present the inward-open structure of a dimeric zinc-transporting P(IB)-type ATPase, resolved at 3.6 A resolution. Biochemical analyses and molecular dynamics simulations suggest that the N-terminal tail, harboring two so-called metal binding domains (MBDs), auto-inhibits the ATPase core and serves as a metal-sensitive sensor, releasing inhibition when intracellular metal levels rise. Contrary to the prevailing uptake models, the structure reveals an electronegatively charged uptake region that directly exposes a metal-binding cysteine of the invariant CPC-motif. We propose that a histidine-rich segment, positioned after the MBD closest to the core, donates ions to the CPC site. Consequently, an intricate interplay between the regulatory and ion-providing N-terminus and the ATPase core is present, safeguarding against zinc toxicity. Collectively, our findings shed light on the regulation and transport mechanism of P(IB)-ATPases, with implications for fundamental biology and the potential to inform future biotechnological and translational applications.

title: An inverse-protein-folding pre-trained model for predicting the mutational effects in protein-protein interactions.
authors: Mao, Sihong; Meng, Siwei; Xiang, Ye
abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) are fundamental to vast biological processes. Accurate prediction of mutation-induced changes in PPIs is crucial for protein engineering and drug discovery. Most existing PPI prediction approaches rely on refined physicochemical features or computationally intensive structural sampling. Here, we present delta-G message-passing-neural-network (DGMPNN), a message-passing neural-network framework for predicting the effects of mutations on PPIs. DGMPNN is pre-trained on an inverse protein folding (IPF) task and employs an adaptive residue-level attention pooling mechanism to enable effective transfer learning for predicting mutation-induced changes in protein binding affinity. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark datasets and deep mutational scanning (DMS) datasets. Experimental validation using computationally selected multi-site variants of the SARS-CoV-2 RBD-hACE2 complex showed strong agreement between predicted and experimentally measured binding affinities.

title: Phytochemical modulation of DNMT1-mediated DNA methylation: computational insights into breast cancer.
authors: Gangwar, Tripti; Jha, Abhimanyu Kumar
abstract: CONTEXT: Aberrant DNA methylation, particularly DNMT1-mediated hypermethylation of tumor suppressor and DNA repair genes, contributes to breast cancer progression. The limitations associated with existing DNMT inhibitors highlight the need for alternative and potentially safer epigenetic modulators. Here, we developed a computational workflow to identify phytochemicals targeting the catalytic methyltransferase domain of DNMT1. Screening of the SelleckChem phytochemical library identified Echinacoside (-9.56 kcal/mol), 1,2,3,4,6-O-Pentagalloylglucose (-9.49 kcal/mol), and Complanatoside A (-9.24 kcal/mol) as promising candidates based on favourable docking and interaction profiles. Among them, 1,2,3,4,6-O-Pentagalloylglucose exhibited most favorable predicted binding free energy (- 105.31 +/- 5.51 kcal/mol) and maintained stable interactions throughout 500 ns molecular dynamics simulation. DFT, PCA, FEL, and QM/MM analyses further supported its favorable electronic characteristics and conformational stability within the DNMT1 catalytic pocket. METHODS: Structure-based virtual screening, molecular docking, DFT, 500 ns molecular dynamics simulations, MM/GBSA, PCA, FEL, and QM/MM analyses were integrated to characterize ligand binding, stability, and electronic interactions. These findings represent purely in silico predictions and require experimental validation to establish the DNMT1 inhibitory potential of the identified compounds and their therapeutic relevance.

title: Structural Snapshots of F(1)-ATPase Catalysis in Drug Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii Reveal Novel Therapeutic Targets.
authors: Le, Khoa C M; Marzinek, Jan K; Mathiyazakan, Vikneswaran; Bond, Peter J; Gruber, Gerhard
journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology
abstract: Gram-negative Acinetobacter baumannii, one of the most critical priority pathogens, has developed multiple defense mechanisms, including upregulation of drug efflux pumps powered by the proton-motive force (pmf) or ATP. As a nonfermenting bacterium, it relies on oxidative phosphorylation, in which the F-ATP synthase, composed of an F(1)-ATPase (alpha(3):beta(3):gamma:epsilon) and F(O)-domain (a:b(2):c(10)), synthesizes ATP, the cell's currency of life. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy structures of the F(1)-ATPase captured during ATP synthesis, revealing concerted conformational changes within the alpha(3):beta(3)-catalytic head that trigger structural transitions of subunit epsilon and twisting of the gamma:epsilon central stalk, coupled with spontaneous ATP formation. Molecular dynamics simulations validate and expand the ensemble of structural rearrangements underlying the rotary mechanism. The resolved intermediate states of the epsilon subunit reveal its role as a molecular gear, regulating ATP synthesis while simultaneously inhibiting ATP hydrolysis, essential for the pathogen to prevent wastage of ATP. These structural snapshots identify novel therapeutic targets and pave the way for rational design of selective inhibitors.

title: Sequence-only prediction of VHH nanobody epitopes and paratopes on HER2 with a frozen protein language model ( ESM2) and a structure-derived residue prior
authors: Dharani Babu; Sundaramurthy Pandurangan; Agilisium Consulting
abstract: Mapping which antigen residues an antibody contacts (the epitope) and which antibody residues do the contacting (the paratope) is central to therapeutic antibody engineering, yet most accurate methods require a solved or predicted three dimensional complex. We address a sequence only formulation: predict the HER2 epitope and the single domain antibody (VHH, or nanobody) paratope from the two sequences alone, with no three dimensional structure prediction at any stage. We pair a frozen ESM2 650M protein language model, used strictly as a feature extractor, with a lightweight trainable module per chain encoders, a shared cross attention block, and epitope, paratope and binder heads (12.2M trainable parameters) trained jointly on three public sources: HER2 binding and blocking competition assays ("AVIDa hHER2" to be published by organizers of SEPIQ 2026 The authors have no right to share the dataset to public ), residue level antibody antigen contacts (SAbDab2), and two reference antibody crystal structures. The blocking competition signal is de confounded into a trastuzumab minus pertuzumab contrast whose sign encodes the HER2 domain and which is used only as a training target, never as a model input. Under a three way, sequence cluster level split with a test set opened exactly once, the binder head reaches PR AUC 0.999 and the paratope head 0.659, while residue level epitope prediction on novel antigens remains near baseline (0.070) a limitation the sealed split exposes rather than hides. Sequence alone recovers the competition derived HER2 domain (the competitor class) for 87.7% of held out clones, a leakage free result. For HER2 specifically, a residue prior built from 25 mined HER2 antibody complexes and validated by leave one out reaches 0.26 to 0.29 residue PR AUC once the domain is correct, roughly 3.6 times the language model head alone. We release and report two submission variants per test clone, a fully sequence only prediction and a competition informed one ,and document which data were used where. Keywords: epitope prediction; paratope prediction; nanobody; VHH; HER2; protein language model; ESM2; cross attention; antibody antigen interface; leakage safe evaluation.

title: DEEP: Extracting Latent Energetic Landscapes from Protein Structure Predictors
authors: Zsofia Borbala Rozsa; Gabor Erdos
abstract: Modern protein structure predictors learn complex sequence-structure relationships, yet the extent to which their internal representations capture the energetic principles governing protein stability and conformational preferences remains unclear. Here, we introduce DEEP (Distogram Encoded Energetic Potential), a general framework that extracts effective statistical potentials directly from predicted residue-pair distance distributions, using the models own terminal distance state as an internal reference without training on experimental stability data. Applied to Boltz-2 (DEEP-Boltz) achieves a mean per-assay Spearman correlation of 0.720 across 64 ProteinGym stability assays, numerically outperforming all 97 published zero-shot methods in the matched comparison on level with the best performing predictors trained directly on experimental stability measurements. Beyond mutation effects, DEEP-Boltz accurately distinguishes native-like from non-native conformations across more than 180,000 Rosetta decoys. Applying DEEP to AlphaFold2 reveals nearly identical conformational discrimination but substantially weaker mutation-effect prediction, demonstrating that recognizing favorable conformations and capturing their energetic sensitivity to sequence changes are distinct properties of learned structural representations. Together, these findings establish that protein structure predictors encode accessible energetic information beyond their geometric predictions and that this information can be extracted. We release the framework and DEEP-Boltz as a freely available tool for extracting these latent energetic representations and for zero-shot prediction of mutation-induced protein stability changes.

title: Projected Gradient Descent for Hallucination-Based Protein Binder Design
authors: Magnus Ross; David Miller; Jude Wells
abstract: Gradient-based hallucination is a popular approach to protein binder design that backpropagates a loss defined on a structure predictor's output to guide optimisation in a continuous relaxation of sequence space, yet the choice of optimiser for this task has received little systematic evaluation. In this work we evaluate simplex-projected gradient descent (PGD) as an alternative to the commonly used gradient descent on softmax-reparameterised sequence logits. By updating amino-acid probabilities directly, PGD avoids softmax-induced gradient attenuation and allows amino acids suppressed early in optimisation to re-enter the design. Using an ESMFold2-based pipeline on ten targets, we find that PGD minimises the design loss in fewer iterations and produces designs with higher predicted interface confidence compared to its softmax counterpart. Simulating selection in real campaigns by considering the upper tail of the ipSAE distribution across a pool of 1,024 designs per target, we show that PGD significantly improves on six of the ten targets, with no significant degradation on any, and produces more structurally diverse designs on every target. Additionally, we find that pairing shorter PGD runs with candidate screening raises the total number of in silico hits per GPU-hour by 29\% relative to default-length trajectories. These results support PGD as a simple and effective alternative for hallucination-based binder design. Code and design data are publicly available.

title: Relation-Aware Graph–Hypergraph Networks for Antibody Sequence–Structure Co-Design
authors: Jinzhu Wei; Shuijun Zhang; Hongliang Duan; Leyi Wei; Jingjing Guo
abstract: The design of antibody complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) is pivotal for therapeutic development, yet remains challenged by the complexity of the antibody–antigen interface. Existing methods, which largely rely on pairwise relationships, struggle to capture intrinsic multibody interactions and global structural constraints. To address this limitation, we propose the Relation-Aware Graph–Hypergraph Network (RA-GHN), a novel framework that systematically unifies graph-based pairwise modeling with biophysical hypergraphs to capture high-order co-operative effects. Specifically, we construct a heterogeneous hypergraph representation featuring three complementary hyperedge types: epitope–paratope interaction patches, spatial structural clusters, and high-degree hub structures, enabling a comprehensive encoding of interface physics. Architecturally, RA-GHN adopts a dual-pathway design that synergistically integrates a Relation-Aware Equivariant Graph Network (RA-EGN) with an Equivariant Hypergraph Encoder , strictly preserving SE (3)-equivariance throughout the sequence–structure co-design process. Furthermore, to mitigate folding hallucination and sequence overfitting commonly observed in generative models, we introduce the Structure–Sequence Decoupling Index (SSDI), which employs a harmonic mean to non-linearly balance structural physical reliability with sequence novelty. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RA-GHN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across standard benchmarks and affinity optimization tasks, validating that the fusion of high-order geometric modeling with rigorous evaluation criteria enables the generation of physically feasible and functionally innovative antibodies. Highlights RA-GHN co-designs antibody sequence and structure via hypergraphs. Biophysical hyperedges capture high-order effects at binding interfaces. Dual equivariant pathways synergistically guarantee local geometry and global shape. SSDI metric addresses folding hallucination in antibody evaluation.

title: Reliable and Efficient Agentic Protein Design with Toolset Harnessing
authors: Jasper Butcher; Jie Chen; Andrew Hunt; Cyrus M. Haas; Wenzhao Dai; Shajesh Sharma; Raktim Mitra; Saman Salike; Jeremy Koob; Aiko Muraishi; Zhe Li; Harley Pyles; Michael D. Tyka; Magnus S. Bauer; Rafi I. Brent; Anant Mittal; Neil P. King; David Baker
abstract: Computational protein design workflows require the orchestration of multiple tools, data formats, and analysis steps that are often fragmented. Here, we introduce Chaperone, a lightweight and customizable framework that enables seamless integration of RFdiffusion3 (RFD3) [1] with downstream sequence design, structure prediction, and evaluation tools, including ProteinMPNN [2], AlphaFold3 (AF3) [3], and more than 50 other protein design tools. By combining a programmable agent-friendly interface with parallelized execution on high-performance computing systems, Chaperone as a harness enables rapid iteration and scalable exploration of complex protein design workflows. Across an evaluation of nine biomolecular design tasks, we find using Chaperone reduces total token usage relative to baseline agents by 86% and GPU costs by 64%, while increasing the overall computational design pass rate. We demonstrate Chaperone’s utility for large-scale design-space exploration through a two-week end-to-end small-molecule binder design campaign, yielding low nanomolar binders to cortisol zero shot. We further demonstrate its versatility across distinct design challenges, including the design of a symmetric 12-subunit self-assembly nanoparticle and a linker that mediates interactions between C2- and D3-symmetric protein complexes to form crystalline assemblies. Together, these results demonstrate how agent harnesses built around standardized tool interfaces can substantially improve the efficiency and success of complex, long-horizon agentic design workflows in biology. We make Chaperone freely available to the community on GitHub: https://github.com/RosettaCommons/chaperone .

title: Distance-AF Multimer: A Multi-Step Approach for Protein Complex Structure Modeling with User-Defined Distance Constraints
authors: Ling K; Zhang Y; Zhang Z; Nakamura T; Kihara D
abstract:
The three-dimensional structure of proteins provides essential insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying their function. Many biological activities are mediated through protein interactions, making accurate structural determination of protein complexes important. Despite significant advances in computational protein structure prediction, there are still many cases where protein complexes are not correctly assembled. In particular, there are cases where experimental data, such as distances between residue pairs in interacting proteins are available, yet existing prediction methods fail to produce models consistent with these data. Here, we present Distance-AF Multimer, a method that guides and refines AlphaFold-Multimer docking predictions using user-provided residue pair distance information. This approach extends our previously successful data-guided single-protein modeling method, Distance-AF. Distance-AF Multimer operates in a two-step process, starting from multiple initial conformations and iteratively refining them to satisfy the provided distance constraints. We evaluated Distance-AF Multimer on protein-complex benchmarks spanning different chain counts and docking errors, demonstrating competitive or superior performance compared to other existing deep-learning-based structure prediction methods. In addition to dimer cases, we also demonstrated the potential of Distance-AF Multimer for large-scale protein assemblies containing multiple chains, including those with more than 5 chains.

Significance Statement

Proteins often function as complexes, but predicting how their components fit together remains difficult. Distance-AF Multimer uses distance constraints between residues to improve the arrangement of protein chains in predicted structures. This approach offers a practical way to combine computational predictions with available structural information, helping researchers study protein interactions, peptide binding, and larger assemblies when detailed experimental structures are unavailable.

title: Computational Profiling and Pathogenicity Assessment of VHL Missense Mutations
authors: R R; Levine E; Roch W; Ciochina A
abstract: Mutations in the VHL tumor suppressor gene promote tumorigenesis by stabilizing HIF-1α. In this study, we investigated the functional impact of VHL missense mutations using AlphaMissense pathogenicity scores, protein stability simulations, and molecular dynamics. AlphaMissense identified high pathogenicity scores for residues 60-200, including the β-domain and HIF-binding domain, suggesting these regions are critical for VHL's tumor suppressor function. We categorized the mutations into two groups: those that primarily destabilize protein folding and those that likely disrupt VHL-HIF-1α binding. FoldX stability simulations revealed high ΔΔG values for both groups, with proline substitutions exerting significant structural stress. Structural modeling confirmed that these mutations disrupt secondary structures, particularly β-sheets. Molecular dynamics simulations showed that the VHL monomer is flexible and unstable in several regions, whereas the VHL-HIF complex, particularly the HIF-binding domain, exhibits enhanced stability. Mutational scanning revealed that bulky amino acid substitutions, such as tryptophan, cause notable destabilization. Interestingly, some mutations predicted to be structurally stable were still classified as pathogenic by AlphaMissense and validated in the literature, suggesting that pathogenicity may arise from subtle functional impairments rather than just structural instability. These findings underscore the value of combining machine learning, structural simulations, and experimental data to predict and interpret the pathogenicity of VHL mutations.

title: Sequence-only antigen context improves modeling of antibody hypervariable regions
authors: Ashraf FB; Lonardi S
abstract: The complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) of antibodies govern antigen specificity; consequently, CDR design should be performed conditional on the target antigen. Most published approaches depend on the availability of the antigen's three-dimensional (3D) structure, which is often difficult to obtain experimentally. In contrast, sequence-only models circumvent this requirement but are typically trained on antibodies without incorporating antigen context; exposure to antigen sequences alone does not necessarily entail learning the underlying interaction determinants. Here, we introduce LangAAI, a masked language model that conditions exclusively on antibody and antigen primary sequences and therefore does not require 3D structures, docking poses, or epitope annotations. To assess whether the model exhibits genuine antigen conditioning, we replace the cognate antigen with a non-binding decoy. Whereas antigen-agnostic models are largely insensitive to this substitution, LangAAI shows a marked reduction in sequence recovery that is specifically concentrated in the hypervariable CDR3 loop. Across benchmarks, LangAAI improves amino-acid recovery relative to existing antibody language models, matches the performance of structure-based methods when evaluated under their respective protocols, and ranks experimentally measured variants by affinity comparably to inverse-folding models that use backbone coordinates. Collectively, these results support LangAAI as a structure-independent approach for antigen-aware antibody optimization, enabling prioritization of candidate variants for targets lacking solved antigen-antibody complexes.

title: RiboDFM: Robust RNA sequence design using backbone-conditioned discrete flow matching
authors: Liu X; An X; Peng Z; Wang W; Yang J
abstract:
Design:

ing RNA sequences that fold into predefined 3D structures is central to RNA engineering, yet it remains challenging due to the scarcity of experimentally determined structures and the complex sequence-structure relationships. Here, we present RiboDFM, a backbone-conditioned discrete flow-matching framework for RNA sequence design. RiboDFM progressively resolves fully masked sequences by integrating a geometric backbone encoder, an auxiliary base-pairing prediction head, and language model representations into a discrete flow sampler. To expand our training data, we supplemented experimental structures with a large-scale collection of trRosettaRNA2-predicted models. Across diverse benchmarks, RiboDFM achieves high sequence recovery and generates sequences with greater tertiary-structure self-consistency than existing methods. RiboDFM also performs strongly on aptamer-focused design tasks. Finally, beyond sequence generation, the nucleotide probabilities derived from RiboDFM' s flow trajectory serve as an intrinsic measure of sequence-structure compatibility. This enables reliable confidence estimation for designed sequences, as well as reference-free, zero-shot assessment of predicted structure models. Together, these results establish RiboDFM as an effective framework for structure-based RNA sequence design.

title: UnibindMD: An Integrated AI and Molecular Dynamics Platform for De Novo Peptide Binder Design
authors: Wu X; Huang A; Fu C; Wang Z; Fu W
abstract: UnibindMD is an integrated computational platform that turns a protein target into validated de novo peptide-binder leads by chaining five orthogonal stages: deep-learning binder design (BindCraft), independent structure prediction and confidence assessment (AlphaFold3-class / Boltz-2), binding-affinity prediction (PRODIGY), developability profiling (ADMET-AI), and all-atom molecular-dynamics validation (GROMACS/CHARMM36m). The platform targets a persistent weakness of single-method design, namely that confidence metrics such as ipTM and pLDDT are self-consistent but not independent, so a design predicted to be confident may still be physically unstable. We demonstrate UnibindMD on three Andes virus (ANDV) intervention points, a setting of urgent need given a case fatality rate approaching 40%, a 2026 MV Hondius cruise-ship outbreak (13 cases, 3 deaths), and no approved therapeutic: the Gn-Gc glycoprotein complex (viral entry), the L-protein endonuclease domain (cap-snatching; PDB 6Q99), and the host VEGFR2 kinase (vascular permeability; PDB 2XIR). Across nine BindCraft campaigns (4,475 trajectories) the platform produced 464 accepted binders (acceptance 2.3-67.6%), with top candidates reaching ipTM = 0.94 and pLDDT = 0.94. The three selected leads were predicted by PRODIGY to bind with G = -9.1 to -11.1 kcal mol-1 (Kd 8 nM-0.2 μM), and all three remained stably bound over 100 ns of unrestrained molecular dynamics (receptor CαRMSD ≤ 2.6 Å, retained peptide fold, ≥ 99.5% of frames preserving more than half of the initial interface contacts, and 75-82% helical content). ADMET-AI flagged the expected poor oral bioavailability of large polar peptides and no PAINS alerts. By converting single-prediction design into a cross-validated, dynamics-tested workflow, UnibindMD provides a rapid, scalable, and generalizable path from any protein target to validated peptide-binder candidates.

title: Conformational Reorganization of a Processive Cellulase on Crystalline Cellulose
authors: Pingali SV; He J; Petridis L; Evans BR; Heller WT; Alekozai E; Cheng X; Lindner B; Smith J; Urban VS; Davison BH; Langan P; O'Neill H
abstract: Enzymes that degrade insoluble polymers must couple catalytic chemistry to productive engagement with heterogeneous substrate interfaces, yet direct structural information on these interfacial states remains limited. We investigated the conformational organization of the processive cellulase Trichoderma reesei Cel7A both free in solution and bound to an insoluble cellulose substrate using small-angle neutron scattering (SANS). Use of biosynthetically deuterated bacterial cellulose allowed the scattering contribution of the cellulose-associated Cel7A holoenzyme to be selectively highlighted using SANS with contrast matching. SANS measurements performed under conditions supporting high or low catalytic activity revealed distinct differences between the free and cellulose-bound enzyme. Under poorly active conditions, the conformational distributions of free and bound Cel7A were similar. In contrast, catalytically favorable conditions produced an additional interdomain correlation in the bound enzyme, consistent with redistribution toward a substrate-selected conformational ensemble. Molecular dynamics simulations showed that free Cel7A samples can assume compact, intermediate, and extended conformations, but these solution-state ensembles did not reproduce the structural features of cellulose-bound Cel7A. These results identify productive cellulose engagement as a structurally distinct state of the Cel7A holoenzyme and support a dynamic model in which the linker and carbohydrate-binding module modulate interfacial positioning of the catalytic domain rather than functioning as a rigid mechanical unit during processive hydrolysis. More broadly, the findings suggest that heterogeneous biocatalysis depends not only on substrate binding and active-site chemistry, but also on interface-selected conformational states that determine whether binding becomes productive. The study further demonstrates how deuteration and neutron contrast variation can reveal functional macromolecular conformations directly within complex interfacial environments.

title: BiHC: Protein domain segmentation by bidirectional hierarchical clustering using Voronoi tessellation and physical self-containment
authors: Le QK
abstract:
Protein domains are commonly regarded as structurally separated, functionally relevant, and evolutionarily separable units. Although classification systems may assign different domain boundaries to the same structure, structural separation remains a shared criterion, and many domain parsers assess it through inter-residue distances, contact numbers, or contact densities. However, the Voronoi contact area, which is widely used to study protein–protein interactions and predict contact sites, has seen limited use in domain parsing. There are two potential challenges to this problem. First, unlike in protein-protein interaction, partitions are not known in advance and must be identified before their interface can be evaluated. Second, the contact area depends on fragment size and internal packing, making it difficult to compare candidate partitions. Here, we introduce BiHC (Bidirectional Hierarchical Clustering), a domain parser based on all-heavy-atom Voronoi contact areas. By normalizing the contact area for fragment size and internal packing, and incorporating residue hydropathy, we define a pairwise self-containment score F. BiHC applies F in two independent hierarchical searches: top-down recursive splitting until no admissible division remains, and bottom-up merging of secondary-structure elements until the entire structure becomes a single fragment. Intermediate partitions from both searches are ranked by a global partition quality score G, derived on the same principle. On two CATH–ECOD consensus benchmarks, under balanced evaluation, BiHC achieved the strongest performance among all tested criterion-based parsers and was comparable to Chainsaw, the best-performing deep learning method tested. These results show that the Voronoi-based criterion can yield competitive domain parsing.

Software availability

https://github.com/LeKhang97/BiHC

Statement of importance

Protein domains are functional units that are structurally separated. Therefore, one natural solution is to identify domains by measuring the Voronoi contact areas among potential fragments. However, potential fragments are not known in advance, and distinguishing candidate partitions is also challenging. This study shows that BiHC addresses both problems using Voronoi-based criteria, providing competitive domain-parsing performance and demonstrating that such criteria can support both boundary discovery and partition assessment.

title: CellTrack-Bench: Microscopic Cell Tracking Benchmark for Vision-Language Models
authors: Ilan Theodoro; Jordão Bragantini; Loïc A. Royer
abstract: Large language models have shown outstanding performance on text-first tasks such as coding, math, and writing. Recent efforts are shifting models' training to include scientific problems that often live in highly specialized domains beyond text, such as protein structure and biological images. However, in these scenarios, their general-purpose accuracy compared with specialized algorithms remains in question. One such domain is cell tracking, which requires spatiotemporal awareness of cell dynamics. To evaluate this, we created a new benchmark, CellTrack-Bench, which assesses Vision-Language Models' (VLMs) cell-tracking-related performance against specialized trackers. The full benchmark draws from 15 standard cell-tracking datasets across four imaging modalities and comprises 1,537 problems corresponding to 9,041 cell-linking decisions. We selected a hard subset requiring greater reasoning effort by identifying failures shared across distinct algorithmic trackers. With this proposed dataset, we: (i) evaluated different environment harnesses for VLMs; (ii) benchmarked 9 frontier closed-source models and 13 open-weight models; and (iii) provided a detailed analysis of their failure modes. Code, the stored model outputs, and a pipeline that regenerates the benchmark from the source datasets are available at https://github.com/royerlab/celltrack-bench.

title: Trion-1: Unifying Language, Protein Sequence, and Structure with Diffusion Language Models
authors: Tianyu Lu; Kaicheng Yang; Jiangtao Feng; Keyue Qiu; Yawen Ouyang; Yixin Wu; Xinbo Zhang; Lihao Wang; Wei-Ying Ma; Hao Zhou
abstract: We envision a general-purpose protein foundation model as a unified, interactive model of sequence, structure, and function, capable of understanding, generation, and cross-modal translation while retaining the instruction-following and reasoning capabilities of modern LLMs. Toward this vision, we introduce Trion-1, the first native, unified, multimodal diffusion language model (dLLM) for proteins. Trion-1 is built on two key design choices: (1) a unified discrete token space that jointly represents sequence, structure, and natural language; (2) a dLLM backbone that replaces strict left-to-right factorization with bidirectional or semi-bidirectional token interactions, enabling global residue communication and long-range contact modeling that are naturally suited to structure modeling. This formulation unifies six core capabilities: folding, inverse folding, sequence understanding, structure understanding, sequence design, and structure design, while retaining the native language capabilities of general-purpose LLMs. On established benchmarks, Trion-1 achieves broadly competitive performance. In folding, Trion-1 achieves a TM-score above 0.8 with a single sample under strict homology control, matching or exceeding the existing tri-modal model using 200 samples. For sequence understanding, Trion-1 performs on par with top-tier LLMs such as Claude Opus 4.7 (62.37%). These results support well-aligned sequence-structure-language representations and strong cross-modal generative capabilities.

title: Can AI Co-Design Structures? An AI Agent for Early-Stage Structural Design
authors: Ricardo Maia Avelino; Mennatallah El-Assady; Tom Van Mele; Philippe Block
abstract: Recent advances in large language models and agentic workflows offer a new paradigm to early-stage structural design translating design intent into structural models. Although text-to-3D approaches have demonstrated that natural language can be used to produce visual, mesh-based geometric models, structural design requires domain-specific geometric arrangements and semantically rich data types. This paper introduces a proof-of-concept workflow for prompt-to-structure generation using an AI agent connected to a COMPAS-based structural modelling API through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Through controlled modelling operations, the agent creates and modifies a graph-based structural data model composed of explicit building elements. The resulting artifacts can be inspected, modified, serialised, and further connected to downstream AEC workflows. The approach is demonstrated through selected prompt-to-structure examples and by progressive and editable design sequences that resemble typical iterative structural design workflows. The results are preliminary, but demonstrate the possibility of combining natural language, agentic workflows, and domain-specific structural data structures as a first step toward AI-assisted structural co-design.

title: RiboBridge: protein-conditioned de novo RNA binder structure design
authors: Zhou Zhang; Hanqun Cao; Minghao Sun; Odin Zhang; Yang Zhang; Pheng Ann Heng; Wujun Li; Tianfan Fu
abstract: Designing RNA molecules that bind to target protein structures requires generating both an RNA conformation and its bound complex geometry, without assuming a predefined binding site. Existing approaches generally model these coupled processes within a unified representation, entangling RNA conformation generation with protein-relative placement. In this work, we introduce RiboBridge, a structure-first framework that separates RNA conformational generation from protein--RNA assembly through cross-frame interaction geometry. RiboBridge first proposes multiple candidate RNA-binding interfaces on the protein surface, generates canonical RNA conformations within a pretrained RNA structural latent space (RiboSphere), and then predicts protein--RNA interaction constraints to bridge the independently defined RNA and protein coordinate frames. The resulting interaction geometry is converted into a geometrically consistent protein-relative pose through rigid placement. We evaluate RiboBridge on a temporally split, sequence-filtered, and redundancy-controlled benchmark of 124 protein--RNA complexes. Under post-hoc interface-correspondence evaluation, where native information is used only after generation to select among already generated predicted-pocket candidates, RiboBridge achieves the highest fNAT and DockQ and the lowest interface and ligand RMSDs among compared methods. Component ablations and stage-wise diagnostics further characterize the contributions of RNA conformational generation, interaction prediction, and rigid placement, identifying the main sources of complex-recovery error.

title: Machine Learning-Enabled Wireless Power Transfer: A Task-Oriented Review of Structural Optimization, State and Parameter Estimation, and Adaptive Control
authors: Denghao Luo; Yiheng Jiang; Jiaqi Zhao; Yuan Gao; Changsong Cai; Weiyi Huang; Yun Zhang
abstract: Wireless power transfer (WPT) systems must maintain efficient and safe energy delivery under variations in geometry, coupling, load, alignment, and operating conditions. Machine-learning methods are increasingly applied to accelerate structural design, estimate operating parameters and states, and support adaptive control and scheduling. This review develops a task-oriented framework organized around three interconnected domains: structural design and optimization, parameter and state estimation, and control and optimization. Supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and hybrid or physics-informed methods are compared in terms of data requirements, dependence on physical models, information sources, computational requirements, accuracy, online response, application scope, and optimization objectives. Supervised learning provides rapid surrogate modeling, regression, and classification when representative labeled data are available. Reinforcement learning addresses sequential control and scheduling but introduces challenges in reward design, safe exploration, and simulation-to-reality transfer. Hybrid methods integrate physical knowledge with data-driven models to improve data efficiency and physical consistency. The principal barriers to engineering deployment include limited and biased datasets, weak out-of-distribution generalization, insufficient physical consistency, unsafe online adaptation, embedded-resource constraints, and the absence of standardized benchmarks. Future research should prioritize uncertainty-aware and physics-informed learning, safe simulation-to-reality transfer, lightweight edge deployment, distributed coordination, reproducible evaluation, and digital-twin-assisted development.

title: Hereditary Effective Atom Theory for Large-Scale Atomic Structure Prediction
authors: Justin Tahmassebpur; Chia-Hao Lee; Cristobál Méndez; Shake Karapetyan; Schuyler Z. Shi; David A. Muller; Tomás Arias
abstract: Predicting the atomic structure of large systems requires simultaneous exploration of atomic positions, species, and, generally, the number of atoms. The combinatorial growth of possible arrangements can make this search difficult even for standard genetic algorithms. We introduce Hereditary Effective Atom Theory (HEAT), which integrates Effective Atom Theory into a genetic algorithm to enable efficient global search through a differentiable effective-atom representation. Central to the method is a crossover scheme that directly superimposes two parent structures and relaxes the combined structure. HEAT outperforms conventional genetic-algorithm baselines in recovering a missing 240-atom H sublattice, predicting a 364-atom edge-dislocation core, and reconstructing twisted-bilayer $\mathrm{WSe_2}$ containing 1150 atoms from ptychographic constraints. These results demonstrate how continuous effective-atom relaxation improves the exploration of large combinatorial structure spaces.

title: VGL-stGen: Learning a shared multimodal model for lung histology and spatial transcriptomics
authors: Haenara Shin; Dongjoo Lee; Sungwoo Bae; Kwon Joong Na; Daeseung Lee; Hongyoon Choi
abstract: VGL-stGen is a multimodal large language model adapted from a pretrained medical vision-language model using paired lung H&E and spatial transcriptomics with single-cell references. Training integrates image-expression and expression-cell-type pairs, and gene-conditioned pseudo-labels transfer transcriptomic cell-type supervision to histology images. One deployed checkpoint supports thirteen evaluated tasks spanning tissue and cell-type classification, gene prediction and conditional expression completion from combinations of histology, cell identity and observed gene expression. Task-specific decoding produces categorical labels, gene lists and structured expression levels. For conditional completion, fixing queried gene identities and predicting their levels autoregressively improves structured prediction. Controlled adaptation shows that restricting supervision to requested expression-level tokens can further improve image-conditioned completion. Image-permutation experiments indicate that correctly paired histology adds information beyond observed expression. External classification relies partly on computational references with shared annotation lineage, and some H&E sources were exposed during cancer training or model development. Within these conditions, VGL-stGen demonstrates how a medical vision-language backbone can learn from spatial transcriptomics and histology to connect tissue morphology and molecular states through shared generative modeling.

title: Curriculum Learning for Generative Flexible Docking
authors: Wenyin Zhou; Hossein Azizpour
abstract: Flexible docking is a highly practical task, aiming to predict the joint configuration of a protein-ligand complex from a protein apo structure and a ligand SMILES string. Diffusion and flow-based generative models have made this task tractable by modeling the posterior distribution over the ligand pose and the protein conformation conditioned on the apo input. The central challenge, however, remains the long-tailed apo-to-holo structure shift, where a small fraction of protein undergo large conformational changes. In this work, motivated by the practical observation that downweighting large shift examples improves generalization, and by the mixed nature of the long tail consisting of genuinely difficult examples and noisy ones, we propose to use curriculum learning for this task, gradually incorporating large conformational change examples during training. With a linear pacing function, we show that an existing method can be strongly enhanced. On the PDBBind ESMFold apo benchmark, with relaxation and confidence-based pose selection, the resulting model GCLDock achieves a 46.52% top-1 success rate (ligand RMSD less than 2A) and 40.26% when additionally requiring PoseBusters validity, outperforming existing baselines.

title: CrystalAR: Autoregressive Modeling for Symmetric Crystal Generation
authors: Ziqiao Meng; Rongsheng Chen; Zhi Zheng; Nikita Kazeev; Zhenkun Wang; Andrey Ustyuzhanin; Wee Sun Lee
abstract: Deep generative modeling has achieved remarkable progress in crystal generation. Given the rich symmetries inherent in crystalline structures, recent work has sought to explicitly incorporate space-group symmetry into generative models, enabling more effective exploration of novel symmetry templates. Yet introducing symmetry templates increases the combinatorial complexity of stoichiometric relationships between atomic species and crystallographic sites, while creating a fundamental tension between flexible exploration of discrete crystallographic templates and faithful realization of these templates as continuous three-dimensional structures. To address these challenges, we propose CrystalAR, a unified autoregressive framework that models Wyckoff symmetry templates and complete crystal structures within a single generative sequence. Specifically, CrystalAR reformulates continuous coordinate generation as a symmetry-conditioned hierarchy of discrete spatial localization decisions, autoregressively refining the positions of all symmetry-inequivalent sites across resolution levels while jointly modeling their spatial configuration within each level. This discrete hierarchical formulation further enables constraint-aware search over both crystallographic templates and geometric realizations. As a result, CrystalAR retains strong symmetry-template generation capability while achieving competitive de novo generation performance and template-free crystal structure prediction (CSP) accuracy. These results suggest that symmetry-template generation can be retained alongside broadly competitive de novo generation performance and competitive CSP without reliance on symmetry templates retrieved from prior data, providing a promising alternative paradigm for symmetry-preserving crystal generation.

title: Ensemble-Aware Structural Encoding (EASE): Conditioning Protein Encoders on Peptide Conformational Ensembles
authors: Ruoyao Zhang; Hongxuan Li; Jie Peng; Tianlong Chen
abstract: Protein foundation models provide transferable representations for downstream peptide prediction tasks. However, existing representations typically reduce a peptide to a single sequence or structure, which may miss conformational variability relevant to key peptide properties, including antibacterial activity, hemolysis, toxicity, stability, and binding. For example, protease resistance correlates more strongly with conformational dynamics measured by hydrogen exchange than with average helicity. Therefore, we introduce Ensemble-Aware Structural Encoding (EASE), a framework for effectively extracting structural information from conformational ensembles for peptide representation. To extract useful information from noisy conformers, EASE selects central conformers representing a peptide's major structural states and fuses their individual representations with a permutation-invariant operator to produce a peptide-level representation for downstream prediction. We then evaluate our framework on six peptide property-prediction tasks under leakage-controlled splits. Against matched single-structure baselines, EASE improves performance consistently on six tasks with a mean absolute gain of about 3.0% across two structural encoders. Gains keep growing as we add conformers through K=20. A single peptide conformer therefore provides a limited basis for structural representation, whereas our framework distilling and fusing multiple conformers yields a more informative representation.

title: EMBER: Predicting TCR--pMHC Binding Without a Docked Complex
authors: Lin Ha; Chen Zhou; Haozheng Luo; Han Liu; Xiaoyu Zhang; Yan Chen
abstract: We propose EMBER, a structure-based framework for TCR--pMHC binding prediction that eliminates the need for a predicted docked complex, and with it the placement error that dominates such predictions. Traditional structure-based predictors utilize the co-folded complex structure of the receptor and the antigen and interpret binding from its contact surface. Consequently, every downstream feature inherits any deviation the structure-prediction tool introduced. Methodologically, EMBER folds the TCR and pMHC independently, encodes them as SE(3)-invariant residue graphs, and compares their learned representations without constructing a shared coordinate frame. A relative pose is therefore not an input of the model, so placement error cannot propagate into the prediction. Computationally, EMBER preprocesses $O(N{+}M)$ monomer folds where a complex-based predictor needs $O(NM)$ operations. Experimentally, under epitope-disjoint evaluation with six retrained baselines, EMBER is first on every metric under all four folding tools, by 0.9 to 14.4% in micro-AUROC, 18.5 to 25.3% in micro-AUPRC and 10.6 to 24.1% in MCC. Its ranking is also up to 85% more stable across folding tools.

title: Doppler-compensated Space-time Coding for MIMO PMCW Radar
authors: Gabriel Daniel; Hanqing Wu; Ashish Pandharipande; Geert Leus
abstract: Phase modulated continuous wave (PMCW) radar is an attractive choice for automotive sensing due to its high dynamic range, interference robustness, and support for integrated communication and sensing. In multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) PMCW radar, code division multiplexing (CDM) separates transmit signals, but non-ideal auto- and cross-correlation properties increase range sidelobes and degrade dynamic range. This paper proposes a Doppler-compensated space-time coding (STC)-based MIMO PMCW radar framework that separates transmit signals before range correlation, eliminating cross-correlation terms under perfect compensation and allowing the same binary sequence to be used across transmit antennas. The Doppler influence on STC decoding is analytically characterized, showing that chip-wise and inter-STC-slot phase distortions increase range sidelobes and generate ghost components in the direction-of-arrival (DOA) spectrum. To mitigate these effects, Doppler is estimated first, followed by joint fast-time and STC-slot compensation before decoding. Residual STC leakage under imperfect Doppler estimation is quantified, and the processing is extended to multiple moving targets through Doppler-bin-dependent compensation.
